title: The Miracle on Ice
text:
In 1980 the Soviet Union had won the Olympic ice hockey gold four times running. Its players were seasoned professionals in all but name. The United States sent a team of college players and amateurs, picked and coached by Herb Brooks of the University of Minnesota. Many of them came from rival programs in Minnesota and Boston who had spent years fighting each other.

Brooks drove them hard and chose players for how they fit together, not just for talent. After a sloppy exhibition tie in Norway he kept them on the ice after the game, skating sprints from line to line until they could barely stand, to make them play for the team rather than for themselves. He gave them a fast, passing style borrowed partly from European hockey.

Two weeks before the Games, the Soviets beat the Americans 10 to 3 in an exhibition at Madison Square Garden. Then, on 22 February at Lake Placid, the two teams met in the medal round. The Soviets led three times. The Americans tied it each time, and midway through the third period captain Mike Eruzione scored to make it 4 to 3. Goalie Jim Craig held on for the last ten minutes under heavy pressure. As time ran out, broadcaster Al Michaels shouted, "Do you believe in miracles? Yes!"

Two days later the team came from behind again to beat Finland and win the gold medal.
lesson: A group chosen and trained to play for each other can beat a group of stronger individuals. Building the team is often worth more than collecting the stars.
people: Herb Brooks, Mike Eruzione, Jim Craig, the 1980 US Olympic hockey team
source: Contemporary reports; Wayne Coffey, The Boys of Winter (2005)
